title: Residential Worksites Reveal H-1B Visa Program Has Become a Cottage Industry
excerpt: A CIS analysis of Bloomberg data finds thousands of approved H-1B visas list private homes as worksites, suggesting widespread self-sponsorship and visa-first hiring.
body:
• A Center for Immigration Studies analysis of Bloomberg H-1B visa data found that in some U.S. zip codes, over 90% of approved H-1B worksites are private residences — suggesting employers are sponsoring visas without actual jobs.
  • Biden-era H-1B modernization rules allowed foreign nationals to start companies and sponsor themselves for H-1B visas, a policy the Trump administration has not yet rescinded.
  • Dubious worksites range from residential addresses and mailboxes to virtual offices, with some single residences listed as the worksite for over 100 approved visas.
  • Critics argue the pattern shows the H-1B program has become a labour import pipeline that displaces American workers, especially recent graduates.

A new analysis by the Center for Immigration Studies reveals that the H-1B visa program has spawned what it calls a "cottage industry" of employers — many of them small, self-sponsored operations — importing foreign workers without having actual jobs for them.

The analysis, authored by CIS Fellow John Miano and based on H-1B visa data obtained by Bloomberg, identifies a pattern of approved visas listing private residences as the designated worksite, raising questions about whether genuine employment exists behind thousands of visa petitions.

The Data: Homes as H-1B Worksites

The findings paint a striking picture. In Aldie, Virginia (zip code 20105), 150 of 151 approved H-1B visas — 99% — listed a residential address as the worksite. In Jersey City, New Jersey (07302), 172 of 181 approvals, or 95%, did the same. In Celina, Texas (75009), every single one of 21 approved H-1B visas designated a home address.

The pattern extended across suburban communities in Texas, North Carolina, Georgia, Missouri, New Jersey and California. In Cary, North Carolina, 80% of approved H-1Bs listed a residence. In Frisco, Texas, 61%. In Santa Clara, California — the heart of Silicon Valley — 23% of 463 approved visas pointed to a home.

"It is clear from the data that employers, big and small, are importing H-1B nonimmigrants without having any actual work for them."

— John Miano, CIS Fellow

Self-Sponsorship and the Biden Rule

The CIS analysis points to a key regulatory change as an accelerant. Under the Biden administration's H-1B modernization rule, foreign nationals can establish companies in the United States and sponsor themselves for H-1B visas and other immigration benefits. Previously, H-1B holders could set up companies and sponsor friends and family, but self-sponsorship was not explicitly permitted.

CIS describes this as "one of many regulations Biden used to create immigration mayhem that the Trump administration has inexplicably failed to rescind." The rule effectively lowered the barrier for visa-first, job-later arrangements, according to the analysis.

A Hierarchy of Dubious Worksites

The report identifies a scale of questionable worksite designations. At the bottom are mailboxes. A step above are private residences. Then come virtual offices, small offices and, at the top, large corporate offices where the number of approved H-1B visas far exceeds the physical capacity of the workspace.

In one case cited by Miano, a 21,761-square-foot corporate office was listed as the worksite for 828 approved H-1B visas — a number that would make physical accommodation of all those workers impossible. Some individual residential addresses appeared as worksites for multiple employers across multiple visa years.

Why It Matters for Indian Professionals

Indians account for roughly three-quarters of all H-1B visa recipients, meaning any systemic issues in the programme disproportionately shape perceptions of Indian tech workers in the U.S. Legitimate H-1B holders — employed at major technology firms, hospitals and universities — risk being tarred by association with fraudulent or dubious petitions filed by small staffing operations.

The H-1B programme is already under significant political pressure. The Trump administration imposed a 00,000 fee on new H-1B petitions last year, and the Department of Homeland Security has expanded biometric screening fees to cover extension petitions filed by large employers.

What's Next

The CIS analysis is likely to fuel calls for stricter enforcement and regulatory reform. Previous attempts to crack down on H-1B staffing companies — including proposals to bar labour brokers from the programme entirely — have stalled in Congress.

For now, the Bloomberg dataset has made it possible for the first time to match approved H-1B visas to specific worksites, providing a granular view of how the programme actually operates on the ground. Whether the data prompts regulatory action or becomes another data point in the perpetual H-1B reform debate remains to be seen.
nri_angle: Indian H-1B holders face reputational risk as dubious petitions from small staffing operations draw scrutiny to the programme that employs hundreds of thousands of Indian tech professionals.
